# Decision on headerless hunks and diffArrays

The initial draft separated "Headerless hunk Parsing" and "`diffArrays` root entry" on the grounds that no conclusion could be drawn from the same sample. The review retained that direction but removed one overly optimistic statement: finding `test/patch/create.js` is not enough to determine the actual handling boundary for headerless hunks by tracing through the test file.

The directly visible items in this file are several adjacent objects on the patch-construction side:

```js
import {diffWords} from '../../lib';
import {createPatch, createTwoFilesPatch, structuredPatch} from '../../lib/patch/create';
import {expect} from 'chai';
```

Among them, `createPatch`, `createTwoFilesPatch`, and `structuredPatch` point to test entry points for patch construction; `diffWords` appears in the same file and only shows that the test file also uses text-diff functionality. Treating these imports as evidence that "a headerless hunk has already been parsed here" was a misreading in the initial draft and is no longer used.

The headerless-hunk record still centers on a direct input and its corresponding output, but the sample should not be assumed in advance to have been produced by `createPatch`. What needs to be checked is whether the old call retains the parsing result for the headerless hunk, so the input should come from a place that passes that text to the existing entry point. The test file is only a review point near the patch-format and construction samples.

`diffArrays` remains a root-entry question. The pass/fail result of a patch test is not used as a substitute for it. What must be confirmed here is whether current dependents can obtain the symbol from the root entry before calling it, and whether completing one call leaves any additional observable changes. Looking only at the export name cannot establish that the caller did not use another path; looking only at a local call cannot establish that the root entry can still be used.

The creation-side observation in JSD-206 is that the old call retains the Headerless hunk Parsing result. The card requires running a piece of source code that directly triggers this case through the existing entry point and saving the input and the tool's actual output. It establishes the correspondence between the sample and the result.

The creation-side observation in JSD-223 is an inventory of the current dependents of the `diffArrays` root entry. The card requires reproducing use of this entry point from the pre-call state and confirming whether any additional observable change remains after completion. It covers the entry point's usage surface and post-call behavior and cannot be rewritten as a patch-parsing task.

The subsequent actions on the two cards also support keeping them separate: JSD-206 has a baseline record and has moved into handling; JSD-223 has gone through interface review and risk review. These actions are not proof of completion, but they show that the two questions have been examined along different workstreams.

This round's decision is to keep two record points: the direct input and output for the patch text are recorded under JSD-206; use of the public root entry is recorded under JSD-223. DOC-16 covers the interface review of Multi-Dialect revision metadata and Array comparator, and can be used to navigate to adjacent topics, but does not replace the judgment here.

# Decision on Hunks Without File Headers and diffArrays

When this page was first written, the upgrade checklist contained two issues that were easy to lump together: the parsing results that existing calls receive for hunks without file headers, and whether consumers could still obtain `diffArrays` from the root entry point. Both arose during 2.x Cumulative Compatibility Upgrade, and both came with pressure to "keep old usage patterns working"; but they concern different kinds of things.

The initial draft handled them separately. That decision stands. What changed later was how the initial draft described where to start verification: at the time, clues near the patch creation tests were described as though the parsing path had already been located there, but a review found that this would mistake "visible adjacency in the tests" for "where the implementation and behavior belong". Accordingly, this record no longer names an unconfirmed location for handling hunks without file headers, nor does it infer the state of the root entry point from patch creation tests.

What is preserved here is a decision about scope boundaries, not an overall upgrade guide. If supporting material is added later, it should be appended separately along the two tracks below; do not fold them back into a generalized "compatibility" conclusion.

## The Original Division Still Holds

The issue of hunks without file headers is defined by what happens after patch text is passed to the existing entry point. The concern is: whether the parsing results that existing calls rely on are still available after hunk text without a file header is passed in. The key evidence here is a direct input and the tool's actual output. Whether the input includes a file header must be recorded alongside them, because that is precisely the distinguishing condition for the sample.

The issue with `diffArrays` is defined by the public entry point and how callers use it. It first asks whether the root entry point can provide that symbol before a call begins, then whether there are any additional observable changes after a call completes. This question does not require patch text to be present, and success with a patch sample should not substitute for answering it.

The two tracks can be handled in the same round, but they cannot share a single vague "pass" record. If one sample includes patch construction, text parsing, and array diff calls, a failure will not tell us which layer changed; if all we have is a screenshot of exported names, that also cannot demonstrate that existing callers still work through the root entry point. Splitting up the evidence adds a little recordkeeping work, but allows each regression point to retain its own shape.

The initial draft compared three options at the time.

| Option | Concerns at the Time | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cover both items with one set of "patch compatibility" samples | Fewer samples, but text results would obscure entry-point issues | Not adopted |
| Keep minimal verification evidence for each item separately | Requires maintaining two separate records | Adopted |
| Wait until all call relationships have been inventoried before writing | Appears safer, but would actually defer existing issues | Not adopted |

The second option does not mean the two tracks are completely unrelated. It simply avoids assuming a relationship: until concrete evidence is available that can speak to both, parsing inputs, the root entry point, and post-call changes each remain within their own scope of assessment.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "hunk without a file header" as hunk
  state "JSD-206" as card206
  state "diffArrays Root Entry" as arrays
  state "JSD-223" as card223
  [*] --> hunk
  hunk --> card206
  [*] --> arrays
  arrays --> card223
```

The two branches in the diagram only show the current record associations. The diagram does not indicate that the two items already share a common implementation-level cause, nor does it present the work actions on either card as final conclusions.

## Misinterpretations left by the initial draft

The initial draft treated `test/patch/create.js` as the "starting point" for hunks without a file header, and there is nothing wrong with that term itself; the problem is that it then described the starting point as the processing location. Here we retain the original reasons for looking at that file: patch-creation objects are directly visible in the frozen test file, and the old investigation notes point here through the issue name and call name. It is useful for further review in the area of patch formats and construction examples.

But the visible contents of the file only go as far as these imports:

```js
import {diffWords} from '../../lib';
import {createPatch, createTwoFilesPatch, structuredPatch} from '../../lib/patch/create';
import {expect} from 'chai';
```

`createPatch`, `createTwoFilesPatch` and `structuredPatch` are objects on the patch-creation side; `diffWords` is in the same test file as they are. This co-location cannot prove where hunks without a file header are parsed, nor can it prove where `diffArrays` is exported from. The counterexample to keep in mind during review is simple: a file can organize tests for both text diffs and patch construction without containing the entry points for either.

Therefore, the old text's connected account of "tracing from the create tests all the way to parsing" should be regarded as an investigation path that has been withdrawn. The test file is still included here to preserve why it was the starting point at the time, not to require later readers to follow it to the same conclusion.

## Scope of JSD-206

The observation recorded when JSD-206 was created is "the old call preserves the Headerless hunk Parsing result". This statement limits the scope to three things: the old call, hunks without a file header, and the parsing result. The card calls for running a piece of source code that directly triggers this scenario through the existing entry point, and saving the input and the tool's actual output.

This requirement does not call for first reconstructing the complete patch history, nor does it require including every possible hunk dialect in the samples. The samples should be straightforward enough: readers should be able to see why a sample is a hunk without a file header, see which existing entry point it was passed to, and place the output alongside the input. If any one of these is missing, the material can at most show that someone looked at a patch fragment, not what the old call preserved.

JSD-206 already had a baseline record, and then moved into processing. This sequence is worth documenting, because it explains why this page first emphasizes "saving the input and output", rather than first listing guesses about where processing takes place. The baseline record captures what was observed at the time; corrections can occur only after processing begins. Neither is an automatic completion marker.

For this line of work, the current decision is:

1. Do not describe a missing file header as an ordinary formatting flaw. It is a condition for selecting the sample.
2. Do not replace input without a file header with a normal file patch generated by `createPatch`. The two have different preconditions.
3. Do not assume that `structuredPatch` is responsible for this type of input, just because it appears in test imports.
4. The output must be the result actually produced by the tool; if no output has been saved, the status can only remain pending investigation.

The last item is especially important. The issue with hunks without file headers is not "what a parser should theoretically be able to accept", but the result of existing calls through the existing entry point. Recasting it as a generic slogan about format compatibility would lose the original regression focus.

## Scope of JSD-223

The observation recorded when JSD-223 was created was "Inventory of current consumers of the `diffArrays` root entry point". The action on the card reproduces the root entry point's behavior starting from the pre-call state, checking whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. It is concerned with how consumers obtain public symbols, and whether changes that should not occur take place across a call.

An earlier simplification of this line of work was not rigorous enough: as long as `diffArrays` could be seen at an entry point, the issue was considered closed. This wording was not adopted after review. Visibility at an entry point only answers whether the symbol can be accessed; it does not establish whether current consumers actually go through that entry point, nor whether a call introduces any additional visible changes. Conversely, finding an array-diff call alone cannot prove that it uses the root entry point, because calling Fang Ke can bypass the public entry point.

Therefore, the record for JSD-223 should retain three adjacent but non-interchangeable segments:

- Before the call starts, the availability of `diffArrays` to the caller through the root entry point;
- The input used by the call itself;
- Whether any additional visible changes occur after the call ends.

This does not require copying a full set of lengthy records for every dependent. The purpose of the inventory is to identify current consumers; the material only needs to make the entry point, the call, and the post-call behavior clear. If only the call can be confirmed for a consumer, but not the path used to obtain the symbol, that gap should be recorded accurately, rather than filled in using another consumer's entry-point state.

JSD-223 subsequently underwent interface and risk reviews. These show that the root entry-point issue was revisited from both the interface and risk perspectives, but this page does not extrapolate from these actions to unknown implementation decisions. For now, they are used here only to maintain the original division of responsibility: root entry-point usage falls under JSD-223; direct text samples of hunks without file headers fall under JSD-206.

## The two tracks should not answer each other's questions

The table below lists the material most likely to be mistakenly interchanged in this decision. Its purpose is to prevent observations about one issue from being used to answer another when adding supporting material.

| Observed material or actions | The limited conclusion it can support | The determination it cannot replace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct input and actual output for a hunk without a file header | What result the existing entry point produced for that input | Whether `diffArrays` is available from the root entry point |
| Symbol state before the root entry-point call | Whether the caller started from the public entry point | Whether the patch text was parsed |
| Visible changes after a single `diffArrays` call | Whether that call produced additional changes | The output shape for a hunk without a file header |
| Patch-creation imports in `test/patch/create.js` | Which tests are adjacent to patch creation | Where parsing is handled or the state of root exports |
| The baseline and handling actions for JSD-206 | The patch-text issue has been tracked separately | Work on the root entry-point issue is complete |
| The interface and risk reviews for JSD-223 | The root entry-point issue has been checked from different perspectives | A particular patch sample has passed |

The boundaries in the table are not intended to reduce verification, but to avoid false positives. Especially with cumulative upgrades, one old usage appearing to remain does not mean that another old usage also retains its original entry point. Conversely, being able to construct a patch sample does not mean that text without a file header is still processed through the old call.

## The proper place for patch-creation tests

`test/patch/create.js` should still be retained as local navigation for this page. It includes the test-level connections involving `createPatch`, `createTwoFilesPatch`, `structuredPatch`, and `diffWords`; these objects help readers understand why the investigation notes were originally placed near the patch-creation side.

The use of this file has now been narrowed to two purposes.

First, when constructing or identifying patch-format samples, refer back to the creation-side objects and test organization. This avoids mistaking ordinary creation output for a headerless sample.

Second, when someone raises the question of "whether this change is merely a creation-side format change", check whether these connections can explain the issue. If they cannot, do not continue drawing conclusions based on the filename.

The third, former use is no longer supported: inferring parser entry points, export hierarchy, or the scope of caller adoption directly from import statements. Import statements show what this test file depends on, not a relationship map of the entire upgrade target.

Nor do we include `diffWords` in the conclusions about `diffArrays` here. Both are names visible in the text-diff toolchain, but the current material does not establish a substitution relationship between them for this issue. Putting similar API names into the same comparison paragraph would only make the root-entry-point question more confusing.

## Trade-offs after review

Three possible ways to consolidate the conclusions were reconsidered during the review.

**First, consolidate under the patch topic.**

This approach initially seemed reasonable because both headerless hunks and patch-creation tests have a patch context. However, it would attach the public-entry-point issue for `diffArrays` to the wrong topic. Consumers of the public entry point do not need to care about hunk formats, and parsing patch text does not depend on the visibility of array diff API. This approach was not adopted.

**Second, consolidate under the API topic.**

Another approach was to include all the `diff*` names encountered in the root-entry-point review. This was not adopted either. The existence of `diffWords` cannot answer the question of `diffArrays`'s root-entry-point status, much less substitute for direct inputs and outputs for headerless hunks. Similar names do not constitute a single compatibility chain.

**Third, keep two cards and one decision record.**

Adopt this option. JSD-206 and JSD-223 each retain the task-level actions; this page records why they cannot be combined into a single conclusion. The cost of doing this is that readers must open the corresponding records separately, but the benefit is that later patches will not mask a gap in the other thread.

This decision does not mean that the two cards can never be linked. If a verification ever establishes that the same specific interface affects both a hunk without a file header and the root-entry consumer, the linked objects and observation result should be explicitly recorded in that evidence, and only then should we decide whether to adjust the scope. The available evidence is still insufficient to make this linkage in advance.

## Withdrawn earlier wording

The passage below is retained as a revision trace:

> Since the patch-creation test contains `createPatch` and `structuredPatch`, parsing of the hunk without a file header should be directly confirmable in the same test track; the root-entry issue can be completed along with patch regression.

This passage is no longer applicable. It compresses the creation side, parsing result, and root-entry adoption surface into a single line of reasoning. The import relationship currently known only shows that the test file is adjacent to both these creation objects and `diffWords`; it does not identify where the hunk without a file header is handled, nor does it provide the root-entry call result for `diffArrays`.

Withdrawing this passage does not deny the value of having started the investigation from that file. The old investigation record did indeed lead the investigation here via the issue name and call name. What is corrected is the endpoint of the reasoning: the file can be a place to continue examining, but it cannot support the entire conclusion without concrete samples or call records.

## Current decision

For now, maintain it as follows:

- Compatibility for a headerless hunk is judged by the direct input and actual output of JSD-206; this page only establishes why it is separate from the root-entry issue.
- The decision on whether to adopt the root entry `diffArrays` is based on the pre-call state, the call, and the visible changes after the call of JSD-223.
- `test/patch/create.js` is a look-back entry point on the patch-creation side. Particularly when `createPatch`, `createTwoFilesPatch`, and `structuredPatch` are involved, test adjacency can be identified from here; it is not a conclusion about parsing ownership.
- Do not use the appearance of `diffWords` in place of verifying the root entry of `diffArrays`, and do not use patch-creation tests in place of enumerating callers.
- DOC-16 handles the interface review for Multi-Dialect revision metadata and Array comparator. That review and this section may both touch on interface wording, but it does not carry the judgments for the two tracks on this page.

The final misunderstanding to avoid is this: "handle separately" does not mean handing the problem off to two places and then stopping thinking; it means not prematurely claiming that they share the same cause before obtaining concrete evidence that can connect them. Regressions in cumulative compatibility upgrades often appear adjacent; only when the inputs, entry points, and results can be clearly linked by the same evidence is it worth recording them as a single decision.

# Metadata Compatibility Plan

This round of 2.x API review recorded two issues side by side: the user-visible entry point for Multi-Dialect revision metadata, and the additional checks for Array comparator. Both may fall within the same batch of compatibility regressions, but don't assume yet that they're the same implementation issue.

`test/patch/create.js` was the closest test entry point found at the time. The file also imports `diffWords`, `createPatch`, `createTwoFilesPatch`, `structuredPatch`, and Chai's `expect`. Adding samples near these existing assertions is safer than changing the public export first; however, these imports only show that the test file references these objects together and cannot determine which helper should generate the metadata.

There are two initial options. The first keeps the different revision forms and pins down the visible text one by one in tests; the second normalizes them to one form before constructing the patch, then has each helper consume the same data. The former leaves more samples, while the latter may wipe out a format that callers previously relied on. Don't casually fold Array comparator into the revision branch either: first confirm whether it is merely a comparison condition for array differences or whether it changes the expected structured patch.

Tentative trial: introduce only one metadata form at a time and inspect the results from the three patch helpers separately; for Array comparator, use independent samples to record the differences before and after comparison. Don't choose a normalization approach before there are samples. If a user-visible entry point does not pass through these helpers, retract the assumption that this can be closed out in the create tests and find another entry point.

# Metadata Compatibility Plan

In May's original plan, revision metadata and Array comparator were placed on the same page because both appeared in the compatibility review of 2.x. At the time, the approach was narrow: add samples near `test/patch/create.js`, then decide whether to normalize metadata. This starting point remains, but it should no longer be treated as a validated implementation path.

## May Original Plan (Retained)

The test adjacency observed at the time was as follows:

```js
import {diffWords} from '../../lib';
import {createPatch, createTwoFilesPatch, structuredPatch} from '../../lib/patch/create';
import {expect} from 'chai';
```

The original judgment was that, since all three patch-construction helpers were in the same test file, revision metadata could first be grouped by helper; Array comparator would get a separate expectation in the array-difference sample. The useful part of this judgment was that it kept the scope of changes near readable tests, and also avoided initially treating the revision text seen by users as merely a header-format issue.

But it also left an overly strong implication: as though completing the samples for `createPatch`, `createTwoFilesPatch`, and `structuredPatch` could determine which entry point owned multi-dialect metadata. Imports in the test file cannot establish that conclusion. It is merely a suitable place to start looking; `diffWords` also appears here, further showing that file adjacency is not a module-responsibility map.

The original plan considered two approaches.

- **Retain each dialect separately.** Leave the expected result for each revision form in place, without having the patch-construction helpers merge them first. The benefit is that old formats remain visible; the drawback is that samples grow as entry points are added.
- **Normalize early.** Organize metadata before generating the patch, then have subsequent helpers use the same data. The benefit is that assertions may be shorter; the risk is that callers may already treat the original spelling, order, or missing fields as visible content.

May selected neither. Array comparator was only written as an "additional check" at the time; there was not enough material to show that it should borrow metadata's branch, data structure, or fallback logic. This point should be retained: two objects appearing in the same review does not mean that one change should close them both out.

## Later Cards Broadened the Scope

JSD-207 records "Multi-Dialect revision metadata user-visible entry-point support". The card requires checking inclusion and exclusion results in the same file tree, without changing global user configuration. This constraint is more specific than May's test proposal: what matters is not only whether a helper can output text, but whether inclusion and exclusion at the user-visible entry point remain stable in the given tree.

The card first underwent a documentation review in September and was then marked blocked because the on-call teammate for Unified Patch Parser was not present that day. The public record left afterward still said that one point in the metadata was unconfirmed and would be updated when the next fact arrived. It provided neither a confirmation result nor which dialect or field remained undecided; "the documentation has been checked" cannot be written as meaning that the parser, patch-construction helper, and user entry point have already reached agreement.

JSD-224 has a different scope: Array comparator addition to the current-version checklist. It requires checking the comparator in an environment without old caches or personal configuration, and recording whether a path was created. The October caller walkthrough at least shows that this check cannot be judged from a single array expectation. The path taken by the caller, whether a path is generated in a clean environment, and the result of the comparison itself should be recorded separately; otherwise, one instance of non-generation will be misread as the comparator not taking effect.

Therefore, May's idea of "closing out both matters together in the create test" is no longer applicable. It remains as the scope-narrowing method used at the time, not the current decision.

## Proposed Trial Boundary This Time

The trial does not attempt to define a specification for all revision metadata, nor does it prescribe new comparison semantics for Array comparator. It only arranges two distinguishable sets of checks and reads the records from both under the same review.

The first set centers on JSD-207. Select inclusion and exclusion cases in the same file tree, while leaving global user configuration unchanged. The record should at minimum distinguish whether the entry point received a particular kind of metadata, whether the constructed patch retained that form, and whether the user-visible result still requires another parsing path to explain it. This does not assume that `createPatch` is the only exit, nor that the fields of `structuredPatch` are the final visible text. If any step cannot obtain revision information, simply record "not reached"; do not use another helper's output to fill it in as a confirmation.

The second set centers on JSD-224. The environment must have no old caches or personal configuration; the sample for Array comparator and the path record should be kept together, but they are not the same assertion. One sample is responsible for showing whether the comparison conditions were carried into the array difference; the other records the path created or not created in that environment. This is not intended to increase the number of tests, but to prevent environmental artifacts from being mixed into the comparison result. The caller walkthrough can help locate the next point to inspect, but it does not itself prove that the comparator is compatible.

The test file is still worth retaining as a local entry point. `createPatch`, `createTwoFilesPatch`, and `structuredPatch` can be used to observe whether metadata differences appear at patch construction; the existing assertion at `expect` is also suitable for a short sample. `diffWords` should not be pulled into this trial unless subsequent review actually shows that it participates in the same user-visible path. May's treatment of a same-file import as a signal that both could be expanded together should now be withdrawn.

## Candidate Approaches and Reasons for Not Choosing Them

**Candidate A: Add per-dialect samples first, without changing the construction logic.**

This is currently the lower-risk starting point. It allows "which form appears from where" to remain in the samples, while avoiding normalization of an entry point that has not yet been confirmed. The cost is that samples may be duplicated, and different helpers' different representations of the same information will be exposed. This cost is temporarily acceptable because JSD-207 still contains one unconfirmed point.

**Candidate B: Normalize metadata before creating the patch.**

May once tended toward using this as a cleanup approach. It is not recommended as the first step of the trial now. If the user entry point needs to distinguish the original dialects, early normalization will leave the inclusion and exclusion check with only one text; the issue will disappear from the tests without actually being explained. This approach is worth comparing again only after the handoffs among the entry point, parser, and construction helper have all been confirmed.

**Candidate C: Bind Array comparator to the metadata branch.**

Do not adopt. JSD-224 provide a comparator check and path record in a clean environment, not a basis for metadata compatibility. Sharing a page is only to let the review see two unresolved regression tracks; sharing a branch would make attribution after a failure more difficult. Array samples should continue to use their own inputs and expectations, without using revision text as a switch.

**Candidate D: Add only the assertion for `test/patch/create.js` and close the review.**

Do not adopt. This file is a valid place to consult, but the scope of JSD-207 explicitly includes the user-visible entry point, and JSD-224 also requires a caller path record. Adding only the local assertion would make the page look complete while bypassing the most specific check conditions of the two cards.

## Record Format

To make this trial reviewable, each metadata sample should retain three short blocks: the input dialect marker, the patch helper it passed through, and the user-visible result or missing result. "Missing result" is important here; it means that the current path did not provide text sufficient for a judgment, and it should not be rewritten as an empty string, a default revision, or successful normalization.

The record for Array comparator uses a different order: first write the clean-environment conditions, then the comparison sample, and finally whether a path was created. Do not treat the path as an annotation. JSD-224 specifically requires recording it, showing that the artifact state of a check is itself information that needs to be reviewed. If the comparison sample does not reach the expected caller, the record should stop at the caller entry instead of temporarily substituting the patch-construction result.

These two types of records do not need to be placed in one large table. The focus for metadata is inclusion and exclusion in the same file tree; the focus for the comparator is the call and path with no caches or personal configuration. Forcing the fields together will only make both sides harder to read.

## Corrections to the Previous Conclusions

The May draft's statement that one should "look separately at the results of the three patch helpers" can still serve as a local observation, but it no longer carries responsibility for choosing a normalization approach. The samples for the three helpers can answer only what each showed during construction; they cannot independently answer whether multi-dialect metadata is already supported by the user entry point.

The wording that "Array comparator records the before-and-after difference with an independent sample" is sufficient also needs to be withdrawn. An independent sample is still needed, but JSD-224 later added the environmental and path conditions. Without checking for old caches and personal configuration, and without recording whether a path was created, a single difference result cannot show that the caller actually used the comparator.

These corrections have not turned the proposal into the current specification. The unconfirmed point in JSD-207 remains, and the blocking caused by Unified Patch Parser's absence that day has not been eliminated by a test adjacency relationship. This page should continue to serve as the trial plan from that time and a record of changes in judgment; when specific task entry points need to be recovered, use JSD-207 and JSD-224 to enter the respective checklist items.

## Withdrawal Conditions

When any of the following occurs, stop expanding samples under this plan:

1. Review finds that user-visible metadata does not pass through any of the currently listed patch helpers;
2. The inclusion and exclusion results in the same file tree can only be explained by parser-side information, while the construction tests have no corresponding input;
3. The comparator check in a clean environment does not reach the path involved in the caller walkthrough;
4. To make both sets of samples pass, Array comparator must be treated as the default or fallback value for revision metadata.

When withdrawing, retain the samples and path records that have already been written; do not delete them as "no longer needed". At minimum, they can show why May started with construction tests, why September did not confirm the user entry point on that basis, and why October added clean-environment and caller-path checks to the comparator check.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Empty Filenames and Paths

This time, start again from `test/patch/create.js`, using its `patch` and `header` samples. Put the original filename, generated header, and output patch in one place; keep an empty filename empty instead of substituting a temporary filename. Record the symptom first, then determine which layer changed.

```text
Unexpected output
├─ Empty filename or path-unescaping change
│  ├─ Already changed before the header: record the original and changed values, stop before generation
│  └─ Header still correct, patch content unexpected: retain the complete output, continue checking the samples
└─ falsey Array Element disappears
   ├─ Corresponding position exists in the output: mark the original array item and the output position
```

# Decision on structured patches and punctuation

The old record of the 2.x compatibility upgrade tracked two issues together: Structured patch Application and Paired Punctuation Boundaries. Both showed up as post-upgrade results that no longer matched the old results, but there wasn't enough evidence at the time to treat them as the same failure.

The initial idea was to put both types of regression into the same set of upgrade checks. The reasoning was straightforward: callers saw changes in text results in both cases, and structured patches could also change the input to subsequent comparisons. That idea was later dropped. Handling them together would mean fewer changes and regression records, but would make it hard to tell whether an output change reflected changes in patch coordinates, context, or paired-punctuation boundaries. In particular, when a patch could be applied but the boundaries in the diff text also changed, a single "results don't match" record wasn't enough to establish the cause.

The decision at the time was to assess them separately. Structured patch Application looks at whether the patch itself can be applied to the target content; at a minimum, the input hunk, target file contents, and result after application must be kept together. Paired Punctuation Boundaries looks at how the diff text encloses adjacent characters, retaining the output from before and after the boundary change. A pass on the first does not imply that the second has no regression; a difference in the second cannot be directly attributed to patch application either. The old claim that "successful application means compatibility" is retained only as a historical judgment and no longer serves as a shared acceptance verdict for the two tracks.

After the split, the recording order also changed. First check whether the structured patch changed the target content, then separately compare the diff fragments around paired punctuation; if both change, do not automatically record the latter observation as the cause of the former. The same input can lead to two different conclusions: patch placement and context remain as expected, while the boundaries around adjacent punctuation still differ; alternatively, the boundary output may be unchanged, but the patch hunk cannot be applied to the target content. These two counterexamples are retained in the history to prevent upgrade discussions from once again treating "successful application" as the conclusion for the entire compatibility chain.

The combined approach was not rejected outright. If the two tracks really are included in the same regression check in the future, they may share a run, but not an assessment: the record must still retain the patch application result and the corresponding boundary output separately. If either is missing, the other cannot be used to fill the gap in the historical assessment. Responsibility boundaries here are also divided by the object being assessed: the structured patch side is responsible for patch inputs, hunks, and where they apply in the target content; the paired-punctuation side is responsible for boundary behavior in the diff text. This division is a record-keeping convention, not confirmation that implementation ownership has been established for either one.

The verification starting point for this page is provisionally `src/patch/apply.js`. From there, the local declarations and adjacency relationships on the patch-application side can be reviewed; this can help with further checks of the handling near `applyPatch`, but the file path alone cannot be used to assign implementation ownership for the paired-punctuation issue. If specific counterexamples are added later, retain the patch application results, boundary outputs, and their respective inputs together. No final test results have been added to this record, and the entry points after the split have not been narrowed down further.

This record stops at that earlier point in time, with the old approach and judgments retained; the unfinished part is the mapping between specific counterexamples, test entry points, and final results.

# fuzzy trial plan

For this API review, we'll first handle the two entry points separately: Bounded fuzzy context during patch application, and the differences in results after the caller passes undefinedReplacement. Both fall under 2.x Cumulative Compatibility Upgrade, but we're observing different things. For the first, we need to determine whether the patch context can still match within a bounded range after the existing text has changed; for the second, we need to confirm what the caller actually receives when a replacement value is missing. A pass or failure at one entry point doesn't settle the other.

## Trial entry point

Start with a small-scale trial in `test/patch/apply.js`. The immediate neighbors currently visible at the top of the file are:

```js
import {applyPatch} from '../../lib/patch/apply';
import {createPatch} from '../../lib/patch/create';
import {expect} from 'chai';
```

This is why we won't create a separate set of entry points in the first round. `applyPatch` is for observing patch application, while `createPatch` is only an adjacent utility for generating repeatable inputs; `expect` still handles the assertions. This file provides a ready-made test location, but it cannot establish on its own where the implementation ultimately resides; that still requires checking the actual references in the corresponding revision.

## fuzzy context: try bounded search first

Change only one variable when preparing inputs: keep the patch content unchanged and change only the context's position in the target text. The record must include more than "pass" or "fail": retain the text of line2, line4, and line5 before and after application, the actual offset, and the final match position. Only then can we tell whether the patch failed to match, matched the intended position, or matched another stretch of similar text.

There are two candidate approaches. Option A probes incrementally by distance, only near the current hunk, and applies the patch as soon as it finds an acceptable position. Its search path is short and its results are easier to explain; the patch may still fail if the context has moved a long way. Option B widens the acceptable offset range so old patches can keep working after more text changes. It may broaden compatibility, but it also increases the risk of incorrect application when the same context appears in multiple positions.

We favor A for this round. The range must be bounded, and the records must show where each attempt stops. Beyond the boundary, retain the failure signal rather than counting similar text farther away as a success. Whether to fix the range through an API parameter or control it only through the test entry point is still undecided; a single example also cannot establish the default order for selecting among multiple candidate positions. If we need to compare B, first widen the range only for trial observation; don't adopt the increased value outright as a public compatibility commitment.

## undefinedReplacement: keep separate samples

Don't treat the name itself as a description of behavior. Each trial must retain at least three original artifacts: the value passed in the call, the comparison target after replacement, and the final diff text. Keep the before-and-after records together within the same operation, rather than retaining only the final result and losing the ability to tell whether a difference arose during replacement, comparison, or output.

Also check the before-and-after states of the working tree and cache location. We don't yet have enough run records to show exactly what the command changed, so we can't classify a particular outcome as stable compatibility behavior yet. If the same input produces consistent results in the before-and-after observations, then discuss whether to include it in the compatibility entry point; if the result still varies with the working tree or cache location, retain the existing behavior for now and pass the differences to the caller for confirmation. These trials only collect API results; they do not decide the business meaning of missing values on the caller's behalf.

## Backout criteria and open questions

If bounded search finds two equally acceptable positions, stop using expanded search; also stop pursuing this approach if line2, line4, and line5 silently end up in the wrong positions after application. For undefinedReplacement, treat either an inability to reproduce the same result from the before-and-after records or an inability to explain which stage produced the change as grounds to back out. When backing out, retain only the original failure signal; don't let a single successful example override the failure boundaries.

Three items remain undecided: whether the fuzzy context range is fixed by an API parameter or limited to the test entry point; the order for choosing among multiple candidate positions; and how to finalize the caller-facing compatibility position on undefinedReplacement. `test/patch/apply.js` is the current starting point for verification, and `DOC-22` separately records adjacent failure boundaries; the two pages can cross-link, but keep the assessments of the two trial targets separate.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Patch Application Anomalies

When a patch application result is inconsistent with the input saved by the caller, or when structured input for a new file gets stuck during application, first retain the patch content used to trigger it, the original text, and the returned result. Do not keep only the content from the last retry; offset search and new-file application can make the same hunk show different behavior at different entry points.

## Split into Two Categories First

If the input is already a structured patch and the target is a new file, follow the "Structured New File Application" branch first. For all other cases, first inspect the hunk's starting position and context, especially when the error or failure occurs only near the coordinates. Do not assess the two types of issue in the same reproduction record.

## Failure Near the Coordinates

Start reproducing with input that has no additional tolerance conditions. Record the hunk's original starting position, the visible context in the target text, and the offset direction and distance used for each attempt. Bidirectional offset Search needs to inspect candidate positions in the forward and backward directions separately; recording only "found a nearby position" is not enough to determine which side matched first.

If both directions produce candidate positions, return to `src/patch/apply.js` to inspect the actual search branch, and save the matched context as well. Do not increase `fuzzFactor` before comparing; otherwise, results from relaxing the context will be mixed in. If neither the original position nor either direction matches, stop treating it as an offset-order issue and investigate the hunk content or the target text supplied by the caller.

## Structured Input for a New File

First confirm whether the caller passed an already structured patch or an object converted from a text patch. For the former, save the object and result that directly triggered application; for the latter, also retain the converted object, so changes during parsing are not mistaken for an application-stage issue.

In the new-file scenario, separately record the file state visible in the input, the hunk content, and whether the target text already contains content. If a directly constructed structured input produces a different result from the caller path, leave that difference for the calling entry point to investigate further; do not rewrite the application branch based on it. If neither side can be reproduced reliably, stop widening the search scope and retain the minimal input.

## End Condition

This round of troubleshooting can end once you can identify whether the failure occurred before or after bidirectional candidate selection, or before the structured input for the new file entered the application stage. If the original hunk or structured object cannot be retained, do not determine the offset direction or new-file handling from a single result; continue after the inputs have been completed.

# Zero-Length Deletion Migration Notes

This record originally served one very narrow purpose: in 2.x Cumulative Compatibility Upgrade, when the target text is empty but the patch still calls for content to be deleted, you cannot determine whether the old and migrated callers behave the same merely because it "looks like deletion". Early records mapped the issue name and call name directly to `src/patch/apply.js`, so many people started investigating from this file. This entry point is still useful, but it preserves the tracing practices used at the time and should not be read as a complete call graph.

The initial draft only required retaining the input and output. The assessment at the time was: whenever the text returned by the existing patch application entry point differed from the expected text, classify it as a compatibility issue with Zero-Length Target Deletion. This assessment later proved too broad. An empty target is only part of the trigger conditions; the same text difference could also come from the hunk start position, a context match, or the structure of the patch passed in by the caller. The old draft did not distinguish these cases. It is retained below to help explain why some older batches left behind very little material.

>
> This rule can still serve as a starting point for investigation, but it is no longer sufficient to determine the migration outcome.

## Objects to Retain During Migration

"Migration" here does not mean replacing one file path with another. The old path is an investigation entry point derived from the issue name and call name; the new path starts with input that can directly trigger Zero-Length Target Deletion, obtains the actual output through the existing entry point, and then traces back to the caller. The two paths serve different purposes: the former helps locate old records, while the latter helps determine whether a compatibility adjustment changed the result available to the caller.

Retain at least four things for each sample to be migrated: the original target text, the patch input, the existing entry point used, and the actual output returned by the tool. Do not represent an empty target with an ellipsis; an empty string and an unrecorded target are not the same situation. Do not extract only the deletion lines from the hunk, either, because follow-up checks often need to establish whether there is context before and after the deletion and whether the result retains the original newlines.

A sample record can be very short. The important thing is to let the next check reconstruct the same set of objects:

```text
Target: empty
Patch: input that directly triggers deletion
Entry point: existing patch application entry point
Output: actual tool output
Notes: whether the caller has been traced back to
```

This does not require filling in a complete execution log for every historical sample. If an older batch retained only input and output, keep it as it is; do not invent a call hierarchy or fill blank fields with guesses just for consistency. What is most easily lost from migration material is "what exactly was passed in at the time", not an abstract statement of failure.

## Moving from Old Records to Current Checks

The actual sequence in the old records was to look at the path first, then investigate the issue. The recommendation now is to reverse that: establish the trigger conditions first, then decide whether the path needs to be opened. This does not reject `src/patch/apply.js`; it avoids mistaking a navigation point for the only place to make a fix.

First, run input that can directly trigger Zero-Length Target Deletion through the existing entry point. There is no requirement to reduce the input to the smallest possible string; if reducing it would lose hunk context or newlines, keep it unchanged. The output must be the tool's actual output, not a description rewritten as "deletion succeeded", "deletion failed", or something similar.

Second, give the same input to the caller that still uses the old approach. If the caller has no separate wrapper, simply record that; if it rewrites the patch or target text before passing it in, save the rewritten values as well. What the migration needs to compare is the output the caller ultimately receives, not an isolated guess about which internal branch `apply.js` will take.

Third, return to `src/patch/apply.js` to check the surrounding code only when there is a difference or the older batch does not specify the entry point. The old investigation records point here from the issue name and call name; the actual relationship still needs to be confirmed against the references in that revision. This limitation applies specifically to this old record: the path can help locate code near hunk application, but it cannot replace tracing through the caller.

Fourth, record which state this sample is in: the old and current entry points produce the same output; the outputs differ but the input is still incomplete; the caller is known to have rewritten the input; or the caller has still not been found. Do not collapse the last three states into "needs fixing". They require following up with different people and inspecting different objects.

The old approach and the approach with the added notes can be understood side by side:

```text
Old record
Issue name / call name
        |
        v
src/patch/apply.js
        |
        v
Guess where zero-length deletion is handled

Current check
Input that directly triggers it + empty target
        |
        v
Existing patch application entry point -> actual output
        |
        +--> Whether the caller rewrites the input
        |
        v
Check back at src/patch/apply.js if necessary
```

The right-hand side of the diagram is not a new runtime flow diagram; it is only the order for collecting migration material. In particular, do not use it to assert that all patches pass through the same hunk application logic. The old records did not provide such a conclusion.

## Handling Older Batches

Early batches usually contain only "Zero-Length Target Deletion" and a source code path. For records like these, first retain the original title, original path, and existing text; do not rewrite them as descriptions of current behavior. Then add a separate migration note: whether input that directly triggers the issue has been found, whether the actual output has been saved, and whether the caller has been inspected.

If an existing sample reproduces the issue but its output differs from the old material, do not overwrite the old output yet. Keeping them side by side is more valuable, because the difference may come from changes to the input between the old caller and the existing entry point. In this case, label the migration record "old output" and "output from this run", and specify which one lacks complete input. Old output without complete input can still help locate historical regressions, but it cannot serve on its own as a current conclusion.

If an existing sample does not reproduce the issue, do not declare on that basis that Zero-Length Target Deletion has disappeared. First check whether the saved target really is empty, whether the patch input still has its original structure, and whether the caller still uses the original entry point. If any of these is missing, leave the record at "sample not reconstructed". The most common misreading in old records is to write "behavior restored" when the issue was merely "not reproduced"; those two statements are not the same.

If the sample reproduces the issue and the caller's output differs, prioritize recording the text before and after the caller passes it in, rather than assigning responsibility directly to `src/patch/apply.js`. This file is a navigation point from the old investigation records, while tracing through the caller was added later. Only by considering both together can you distinguish a change in the existing entry point's own result from a change in the objects passed in by the outer layer.

## Migration Batches That Can Still Be Used

Batches do not need to be divided by repository directory. Samples with complete material are suitable for migration first: an empty target, a patch that directly triggers deletion, and output from the existing entry point. Even if the caller has not yet been found, these samples can establish the "actual tool output" first.

Migrate samples from old callers in the second batch. The focus here is not on collecting more hunks, but on confirming whether the caller processed the target text or patch input. If it did not rewrite them, simply record "no rewriting observed"; if the material cannot establish this, leave it unknown. Do not invent a caller name or wrapper step just because the old path points to `apply.js`.

Only in the third batch should you handle old records that have a path but no input. There is a reason these records remain in the material: they can still lead people back to the old investigation location. But without input that directly triggers the issue, they cannot be included in completed compatibility checks. You can add "original input still needed" beside the path; there is no need to create a similar case on the spot just to close out the batch.

Keep the completion criteria narrow for each batch as well: the input, empty target, and actual output can be viewed side by side; if an old caller is involved, the record can state whether the caller has been traced. Completion does not mean that every internal handling location has been identified, nor that every guess in the old records has been confirmed.

## Returning to the Old Entry Point

When migrated samples cannot explain a difference, restoring the old path does not mean undoing all the work. It means narrowing the scope of the check back to the objects that could originally be confirmed. Retain the input and output already collected, then start investigating from the issue name, call name, and `src/patch/apply.js` in the old records. Do not delete the "current entry point output" when restoring the old path, or next time there will once again be nothing but a path and a conclusion.

After restoring the old entry point, first ask three local questions: whether the target is empty; whether the patch can still directly trigger deletion; and whether the caller uses the same entry point as when the output was saved. If material is missing for even one of these three questions, mark this restoration as incomplete and do not continue inferring specific implementation causes.

A common practice in the old workflow was to look for hunk handling near the source code path first, then work backward to the input. This can still help with reading the code when the material is complete; when migration fails, however, it can easily lead people to assign a cause first and then select samples that support that attribution. This record therefore retains it as a follow-up checking step, rather than the first step in every check.

## Review Addendum

A later review added the step of tracing through the caller and used JSD-214 as a navigation card. The card stores the input and actual tool output from running a piece of source code that directly triggers "Zero-Length Target Deletion" through the existing entry point. This means the old records no longer depend solely on a path, but it does not provide a single conclusion covering all callers.

There was one assignee change during the review. This change does not indicate that technical ownership has been settled; it only means that subsequent material needs to expand beyond simply locating source code to checking whether the caller changes the input. If the related result says only "handed over", it loses the information about why the old path still needs to be retained.

For now, this page should still be used as an old migration record. It is suitable for handling historical samples of Zero-Length Target Deletion, saving outputs side by side, and recovering the old investigation entry point; it is not a substitute for complete patch application documentation. If a new issue has only a text difference and no empty target, it should not be classified directly using this page's old rule.

One related question remains: when an old sample's output contains newline differences, should it be checked in the same batch as Zero-Length Target Deletion, or should a separate record be created? There is currently not enough material to decide.

# Multi-file callback decision record

The scope here is Multi-File callback Order, not a compatibility note for all diff API. The earlier investigation followed the issue and call names to `src/index.js`, so this record first pins down the starting point for verification, then determines which ordering is public behavior and which is merely internal implementation ordering.

## The choice

At the time, there were two options: let each file invoke its callback through its own call path and leave callers to adapt, or handle callback ordering for multi-file results at a unified entry point so callers can rely on one stable order. The first approach would involve fewer changes, but files in the same batch could finish in different orders, making it hard for callers to distinguish "the file hasn't been processed yet" from "the callback has already finished." The second approach was closer to addressing the problem the compatibility upgrade needed to solve, but required confirmation that the unified entry point actually controlled scheduling for these files.

This page adopts the second option as the working decision for further verification: check Multi-File callback Order at the unified entry point, rather than defining separate rules in each diff algorithm file. This decision does not establish that the current implementation satisfies that order; until we have seen the call chain and actual callback records, the order must not be documented as a published behavioral guarantee. If verification shows that callers assemble the order, we need to return to option one and reassess, rather than using the entry-point filename as a substitute for evidence.

## Local relationships at the entry point

The file header of `src/index.js` lists several groups of adjacent imports:

```js
import Diff from './diff/base';
import {diffChars} from './diff/character';
import {diffWords, diffWordsWithSpace} from './diff/word';
import {diffLines, diffTrimmedLines} from './diff/line';
```

These declarations show that character-, word-, and line-level functionality can be explored from here, but they do not themselves establish the execution order of multi-file callbacks. The import of `Diff` also does not, on its own, prove that it handles file scheduling. The investigation should trace further down from this entry point's exports and direct call relationships to establish "where the file list enters, how each completion is reported, and when the next file starts." This page uses these only to bound the search; it does not present adjacent imports as confirmation of implementation ownership.

## Ownership boundaries

core is responsible for confirming whether the unified entry point controls the order and whether changes to that order would affect existing callers; integration only needs to provide examples of calls that actually depend on multi-file callbacks and the order in which callbacks are received. Integration must not infer this from single-file diff results. Until the rules are confirmed, the compatibility upgrade should not encode callback order in new calling code as an implicit cross-module assumption.

We still need a record of actual behavior that pins down "which file gets its callback first, and whether processing continues after an exception." Once that record is found, add only the specific order and exceptions; without a record, retain this decision and do not turn guesses into an interface commitment.

# patched acknowledgement proposal

The patch-creation side has not yet clearly defined what the patched acknowledgement is responsible for. Proceed with a narrow assumption: the acknowledgement only records that one patch creation has been handed off to the caller; it does not indicate that the patch has been written, applied successfully, or that subsequent files have finished processing.

The existing test entry point is at `test/patch/create.js`. The file also imports `diffWords`, along with `createPatch`, `createTwoFilesPatch`, and `structuredPatch`; this shows that several forms of the creation result are checked in the same place, but that alone does not mean all creation functions belong to the same acknowledgement chain.

Try two candidate points first:

- After the patch text or structured result is formed, issue an acknowledgement; have the caller invoke Fang Ke and use the acknowledgement as the signal that this creation is complete.
- Do not add new acknowledgement semantics; let the caller use the existing result as the basis for completion.

The first makes it easier to place the test on the creation side, at the cost of callers readily reading "creation complete" as "the patch has been applied." The second avoids that ambiguity, but the name remains with the caller, so interface reviews will keep asking what exactly it confirms.

Do not include format differences, text diffs, or subsequent multi-file processing in this trial yet. If implementation requires changing the synchronous creation path to an asynchronous one, or if the acknowledgement only makes sense at the application stage, withdraw the creation-side proposal.

# patched acknowledgement proposal

Initially, patched acknowledgement was tentatively treated as a signal that "patch creation has been handed off to the caller." That wording remained in the previous version because the discussion at the time was about whether the creation side needed a visible endpoint; it did not distinguish between patch content being produced, the caller receiving that content, and any subsequent application or multi-file orchestration by the caller.

The review only revisited the creation-side context around `test/patch/create.js`. The imports at the top of the file are:

```js
import {diffWords} from '../../lib';
import {createPatch, createTwoFilesPatch, structuredPatch} from '../../lib/patch/create';
import {expect} from 'chai';
```

This supports only a narrow conclusion: text patches, two-file patches, and structured patches share a test entry point here; `diffWords` is also available in the same test file. It does not prove that any of these functions emits an acknowledgement, much less that acknowledgement and patch application belong to the same layer. The previous version made "tests can live on the creation side" sound like a decision about interface ownership. This should be changed back to a trial condition that still needs to be verified.

## The ambiguity to resolve here

Different callers can easily interpret `patched` in the name as one of three stages:

1. A patch representation has been generated;
2. That representation has been handed back to the current caller;
3. A downstream path has actually processed the patch.

The previous version leaned toward the second meaning, not because it had been validated in the implementation, but because it does not require the creation module to claim any application outcome. If the acknowledgement ultimately stays on the creation side, both the wording and the tests should cover only the second meaning. What the caller does after receiving the acknowledgement remains on the caller's side of the boundary.

The first meaning looks close to the second, but would require separate explanations of when "generation" is complete for structured and text results; this proposal should not assume that the return forms of `createPatch`, `createTwoFilesPatch`, and `structuredPatch` are the same kind of acknowledgement carrier. The third meaning goes directly beyond the entry point being examined here: it requires looking at actual callers and application paths, and cannot be inferred from the creation test file.

## Candidate approaches for a trial

**Candidate A: Acknowledge when the creation result is delivered.**

Once the creation function has finished constructing its result, the caller receives an acknowledgement. The advantage is that the signal is close to something testable, and text and structured results can have separate assertions. The drawback is also clear: if users take it to mean "already applied," the name alone cannot prevent that misreading. Continue with this approach only if callers are confirmed to actually need a creation-complete signal.

**Candidate B: Do not add an acknowledgement at the creation layer.**

Continue treating the existing returned result as the basis for determining that creation is complete. Leave patched acknowledgement in the higher layer that actually needs to orchestrate subsequent work, rather than attaching an overly broad term to the creation module. The advantage is that there are no new timing commitments; the cost is that the higher-layer entry point still needs to be found, or the problem is merely postponed.

**Candidate C: Put the acknowledgement at the end of processing.**

This was previously raised as an option with "a more intuitive name," but no material available so far connects the creation test entry point to the actual end of processing. It would also tie creation, application, and multi-file ordering to a single signal. Unless further investigation finds a clear caller dependency on this stage, it should not be used as the basis for changing the creation-side interface.

Of the three, A is only a starting point for a trial, not a finalized interface design. The previous version did not make this clear, which could lead readers to think that `test/patch/create.js` already covers the full acknowledgement chain.

## Samples to examine during review

The trial does not need to expand into a rework of all patch behavior at the outset. First, look separately at whether text patches and structured patches can express the same thing when creation completes: whether the caller has obtained the result. Include two-file patches only if their result delivery point differs from that of single-file patches; do not automatically treat them as the same case just because they are imported by the same file.

Tests should observe result content and the acknowledgement separately. Content format should still be constrained by the creation functions' own assertions; if an acknowledgement exists, check only that it does not encroach on the semantics of the caller's subsequent processing. The import of `diffWords` is not grounds for expanding this proposal. It is merely an adjacent item in this test file and should not be a reason to bring text diff output into the interface's scope.

What needs to be established is not "whether there is a term called patched," but whether a real caller, after receiving the creation result, needs to distinguish between continuing execution and having finished processing. If that caller only consumes the return value, Candidate B is more appropriate than an extra signal; return to A only if it actually waits for ordered delivery, and limit the acknowledgement to delivery, without terms such as success or application complete.

## Retained withdrawal conditions

Stop the creation-side trial if any of the following occurs:

- Emitting an acknowledgement requires changing how the existing synchronous creation functions are called;
- The same acknowledgement can only be explained in terms of different stages for text results and structured results;
- The caller found actually cares about patch application rather than delivery of the creation result;
- The acknowledgement needs to commit to an order for processing multiple files.

Withdrawing does not mean patched acknowledgement has no use, only that it should not be the responsibility of the patch creation test entry point. At that point, take the question to the actual caller: is the acknowledgement for result delivery, a single application, or completion of the entire batch?

Two items are still missing: the caller entry point using this term, and the version-specific results that entry point relies on. Without both, Candidate A cannot be promoted to a stable interface, nor can creation-side tests be used to draw conclusions on the caller's behalf.

# Quality Signal Cache Trade-off Record

The earliest decision preserved in this record was a very narrow one: when the Quality Signal Dashboard already had the captured state for the current revision, no additional environment would be rebuilt just to fill in the background. The cache could be kept, but the original captured state also had to be preserved. That judgment did not mean the cache could always be trusted, much less that every future investigation should follow the same entry point.

The initial draft divided the problem into two layers. One was how to preserve the captured state; the other was where the signal began to change. For the latter, what was on the table at the time was not a complete implementation overhaul, but two closely related options: continue examining everything through `structuredPatch`, or split out `fuzzFactor` and examine the failure exits it passes through separately. The draft chose the latter for a simple reason: the two segments already had different failure exits, and continuing to treat them as the same kind of signal would flatten the comparison.

The "rebuild first, then judge" approach was not adopted at the time. This was not because rebuilding was necessarily ineffective, but because the original command parameters had not been recovered. Without them, a rebuilt environment could only show what happened under a different set of conditions; it could not replace the captured state already preserved. The current revision was therefore fixed as the comparison point for the time being; if the complete parameters were recovered later, the rerun was to be recorded on a separate line, not silently overwrite the original record.

The trade-off between the cache and the original captured state was therefore also made very conservatively. The cache was useful for taking people back to the fragments preserved at the time, especially when revisiting the same revision; the original captured state preserved the failure sample itself and its context at the time. A green result after cleanup could not replace the original captured state. This statement was intended to prevent differences between failure exits from being erased if only the cleaned-up results were retained, not to draw conclusions about cache performance or retention periods.

## Two Gaps Left by the Initial Draft

The current callers of `CommonJS export` had not been fully identified. This was noted here because any change to the shared entry point would make the trade-off about captured state affect callers, and there was no material at the time that could settle the matter. The other gap concerned rollback: if a rollback became necessary after splitting out `fuzzFactor`, would it be enough to restore only the old entry point? The draft had no answer.

There were objections at the meeting, but these notes did not transcribe the reasons for them one by one. Preserving that fact is more appropriate than adding a seemingly complete rationale. The objections were not withdrawn, nor did they become a new decision in the subsequent material.

## Record of Later Actions

Several different kinds of work were later carried out around this page, and their sequence matters more than any individual action. First came a comparison of approaches, followed by a rerun under fixed conditions; the work status was then advanced, and the interface scope was also reviewed, before the scope following reassignment was finally confirmed. These actions do not automatically prove that every conjecture in the initial draft was correct; they only show that the decision was tested against actual maintenance issues.

JSDA-007 made "the complete command is missing" more than just a reminder at the meeting. The card required recovering the complete command used at the time and recording the results obtained with the later-supplied parameters on a separate line. No command has been fabricated here on that basis, nor have the later results been merged back into the original sample. The original judgment remains: when parameters are missing, output from a new environment cannot be described as a reproduction of the old captured state.

JSDA-011 record another, more constrained approach: keep diff-quality-signal, the current entry point, and the command fixed, and change only the current revision. This addresses whether revision is a variable worth comparing on its own, rather than making environment rebuilding the only means of verification. The initial draft's choice to "retain the current revision" therefore remains understandable, but its applicability should be limited to comparisons under these fixed conditions.

JSDA-013 brought the issue of the old entry point to light. After the window closed, the current entry point still had the old value; the card required checking again whether it came from the old cache or the old task. The material did not reach a final conclusion about its source. This also means that an entry point cannot be treated as a still-valid reference to the captured state merely because it remains displayed on the page. The original cache arrangement did not answer this question.

Even after the interface review, the original choice to leave `CommonJS export` unresolved remained appropriate: reviewing the interface side did not mean the current callers had been fully listed. The initial draft did not record the interface review as approval for migration, nor did it authorize changes to the shared interface on that basis. That part remained unresolved.

Scope confirmation and maintainer reassignment came later. The record in JSDA-009 only required handing the branches after the current entry point to the current maintainer once diff-quality-signal was confirmed to be usable. It did not redefine how long the original captured state should be retained, nor did it make the cache the sole evidence. The original wording "the branches that follow" is retained here because it indicates that the reassignment covers the part after the entry point, rather than moving the earlier captured state in its entirety.

## Exit Wording That Is No Longer Valid

The initial draft listed "whether to restore only the old entry point" as a rollback question. At the time, this was still open to discussion because the entry-point hint on the page was assumed to be usable. A later card note explicitly stated that the expiration action was no longer effective, while the entry-point hint on the page had not yet been updated.
